questions.stem: Engineer Vic writes a brief note explaining how momentum informs a crash barrier design.

answer.exemplar: The barrier must absorb the vehicle's momentum by extending impact time, reducing peak force. Momentum conservation guides the required impulse and energy dissipation targets.

questions.explanation: Momentum sets the impulse the barrier must manage. Extending time reduces force for a fixed momentum change.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Explain impulse in a design brief
questions.stem: Engineer Wes writes a brief note explaining impulse in a hammer strike design.

answer.exemplar: The hammer delivers impulse by applying force over the strike duration, changing the nail's momentum. A heavier or faster hammer increases impulse and drives the nail deeper.

questions.explanation: Impulse equals force times time and changes momentum. Design choices scale impulse delivered.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Explain conservation in a design brief
questions.stem: Engineer Xan writes a brief note explaining momentum conservation in a docking mechanism.

answer.exemplar: During docking, no external force acts, so total momentum is conserved. The mechanism must manage relative velocities so the combined craft moves at the conserved total momentum.

questions.explanation: Isolated docking conserves momentum. Design must account for shared final velocity.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I
questions.learningObjective: Explain collision type choice in design
questions.stem: Engineer Yara writes a brief note explaining why a bumper uses inelastic design.

answer.exemplar: An inelastic bumper absorbs kinetic energy by deforming, reducing rebound and protecting occupants. Elastic designs would bounce vehicles back, increasing collision severity.

questions.explanation: Inelastic absorption converts kinetic energy to deformation, reducing rebound. This improves safety.
